title: Label Inconsistency Investigator
content:
Purpose: Quick investigation scratchpad for recurring label inconsistencies we've observed when cleaning and labeling inbound user-generated content (UGC). This is personal notes + short experiments to turn into a small checklist and a compact rubric for reviewers. Aim: reduce disagreement on edge cases, make propagation for corrections reproducible, and detect drift early. Context / why this matters: - We have ~8% inter-annotator disagreement on 'entity span vs description' cases for UGC in the last batch. - Several noisy variants: HTML-embedded snippets, Markdown with inline code, translated strings (machine + user), and multilingual punctuation differences. - Quick fixes have been ad-hoc; need a lightweight, reproducible set of rules and sample-driven testcases for reviewer calibration. Observed failure modes (examples): 1) HTML attribute text:
... - Some reviewers label the title attribute as product-title entity, others ignore because it's metadata. - Decision hinge: Is the text rendered to end user? title shows on hover; treat as candidate only if visible in render. 2) Markdown inline code: `product_123` vs plain text product 123 - Code spans often indicate IDs; some labelers treat as labelable entity, others abstain. - Heuristic: if it's a stable ID pattern (alpha+digits) and downstream needs ID extraction, mark as ID-ENTITY. Otherwise abstain. 3) Translated UI fragments: \"envío rápido\" (es) vs \"fast shipping\" - Inconsistent mapping when English rubric exists. Two problems: (a) missing language normalization; (b) reviewers inferring canonical English intent. - Rule: label in-source-language; add normalization tag when needed. Only map to canonical English in a separate normalization pass. 4) Multiline user signatures and footers - Long spans often lead to overspecific entity spans. Some reviewer's spans include punctuation and salutations. - Rule: trim polite salutations and trailing contact lines unless they are explicitly requested as part of labeled field. Propagation and correction rules (lightweight): - When correcting a label that is a tokenization/boundary issue, add an explicit correction note (comment) describing the tokenization change and file the correction into the corrections.csv with columns: example_id, original_span, corrected_span, correction_type (boundary|format|language|semantic). - If >5 corrections of the same correction_type in a batch, schedule a quick pattern-based auto-fix script (see automation notes below) and flag to reviewers. - For translated content, corrections should not change language; add a language_hint tag and keep mapping to canonicalization separate. Reviewer calibration mini-protocol: - Create calibration batches of 25 diverse examples with 1-2 known contentious examples (HTML attr, inline code, translated phrase). - Measure reviewer agreement / calibration score; if <75% agree with gold, require a 20-min sync and re-training. - Maintain a small living doc (calibration_examples.csv) with gold annotations and rationale for 50 canonical edge cases. Sampling queries to surface the worst offenders: - regex: <[^>]+title= to find title attributes in HTML - markdown backticks: `[^`]+` - unicode punctuation clusters: [\u2018\u2019\u201c\u201d—–]{2,} - language detection flag: lang_confidence < 0.8 Quick heuristics (to be encoded in a lightweight linter): - If span contains HTML attribute and attribute value not part of rendered DOM text -> mark as metadata, suggest abstain. - If span wholly inside inline code and matches ID regex (^[A-Za-z_\-]{2,}\d{2,}$) -> suggest ID-ENTITY. - If span length > 160 chars and contains salutations (\"thanks\", \"cheers\", \"regards\") -> suggest trimming to first sentence. - If machine-translation detected and language != project_language -> tag language_hint:XX and abstain from canonical mapping. Automation snippets (notes for infra/dev): - corrections.csv auto-aggregator: simple lambda that collates corrections and emits top-10 correction patterns per week into a GitHub issue. (linked PR above is a start). - linter prototype: node script that runs above heuristics and outputs suggested actions as comment annotations in the labeling UI. Minimal false positives preferred. Examples for the calibration doc (short list with rationale): - Example A: \" New release\" -> Label: \"New release\" only; alt used for image description only if UI shows it. - Example B: \"Order ID: `ORD_0072`\" -> Label: \"ORD_0072\" as ID-ENTITY. - Example C: \"envío rápido (ℹ️ información)\" -> Label: \"envío rápido\" as shipping-term (in Spanish); add language_hint:es Open questions / things to try: - Should we unify by canonicalizing punctuation (smart-trim) before labeling? Pros: reduces boundary noise. Cons: may mask truth in user text. - How aggressive should linter suggestions be vs auto-fixes? Start conservative (suggest only). - Can we incorporate a tiny transformer-based consistency check (embedding-based) to detect when two labels across translations are likely same semantic item? Follow-up: small eval experiment. Actionable next steps (my plan): - Draft a one-page rubric from this scratchpad (deliverable: rubric-v0.1.md) by end of week. - Build 50-example calibration set and run with 6 active reviewers (Evan & Lina as seeds). - Wire corrections.csv output into the aggregation job (file an infra ticket). - Prototype the linter on a 1k sample and measure precision of suggestions. Notes to self: - Keep decisions minimal and explicit: always say why we keep or drop a span. That rationale is the most valuable training signal for annotators. - Watch for drift after model updates/labeler churn; schedule monthly quick audits. End of scratchpad. -- Maya
